title: The AI Frontrunner Is Just a Refinery, Not the Native-App Winner
dek: AI has entered its agent phase: the first-stage leaders are just refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations must shift from roles to tasks; and in the end what people compete on is the creativity to conjure something from nothing.
why: Zeng Ming gives you a coordinate system for locating where AI sits today, built on a three-stage industrial history. It is a specific cure for ‘this time is different’ optimism, and it hands application founders their window of opportunity along with a brutal forecast for how incumbents will transition.
who: CEOs working out AI strategy, executives at traditional giants hunting for a second curve, AI investors, and technical founders torn between building models and building applications.
skip: The rapid-fire Q&A and book list at the end can be skipped (after 2:29).

points.h: Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
points.body: Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of a general-purpose technology into three stages: first it becomes social infrastructure, then applications explode, and finally native applications appear. In 2026, token as a unit of measurement reached consensus, which shows the first stage has matured; the agent events around Chinese New Year (commonly called ‘lobster’) mark AI's formal entry into the agent stage. He draws the analogy to the 1992 website-building movement: people then were building websites to share information, people today are building agents to share capability. The browser hasn't appeared yet, and whoever can establish the agent standard and seize the user entry point may hold the biggest opportunity of the next two years.

points.h: A ten-trillion-dollar company will appear, but not these two
points.body: Zeng Ming says plainly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technological and commercial achievements, but business history shows the first wave of breakout companies is most likely not the big winners of the native-application stage. Yahoo reached a $120 billion market cap five years after founding, AOL was valued at $220 billion, and neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies, refineries that refine the base oil; the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies — and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will certainly exist in the future, but it may not be the two currently leading. Model companies will move toward a mature business of oligopoly plus heavy government regulation.

points.h: The unit of an AI-native organization is the task, not the role
points.body: The company corresponds to the bureaucracy of the industrial age; AI overturns the industrial age, and the corporate system will wither. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not the role but the task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow around ‘what problem needs solving’, and humans and AI coordinate around tasks. So well-designed roles and hierarchies will disappear, and the traditional middle layer will die too; future founders must first define the organization's task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of the new organizational form, and OpenAI itself looks more like a Lab than a traditional company. The culture of the new organization is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing and co-creation, no longer relying on commands and performance reviews.

points.h: Excellence is only judged in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
points.body: Zeng Ming argues that ‘good ≠ great’. Being good is growth that keeps receiving positive feedback, while greatness requires overcoming negative feedback again and again, persisting when no one approves, and finally proving through enormous success that you were the era's earliest prophet — which is why ‘greatness is judged in hindsight’. Good people fall very easily into a loop of proving themselves, which makes their strategies conservative. Great people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the era and their partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When he identifies founders he asks, ‘Ten years from now, what kind of self would you be satisfied with?’ If the answer is ‘build a ten-billion-dollar company’, that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly great founders tend to be altruistic and empathetic.

points.h: Strategy in the AI era can't be planned, only generated
points.body: Strategy in the AI era is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a ‘strategy generation system’: the organization must build an environment and a network in which strategic insight emerges naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are higher, a CEO cannot plan by linear extrapolation, nor can strategy be outsourced to McKinsey — McKinsey's explosion was a product of the slow maturity of the industrial age. His methodology is ‘look ten years out, think three years out, act one year out’, and the core is ‘think three years out’: you must at least see two or three milestones so that short-term action and the mid-term picture create tension. Organization building must guarantee a large enough context rather than control, letting the right people make the right decisions at the right time.

points.h: The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
points.body: Zeng Ming believes robotics is still in a phase of strategic exploration, far from convergence. Of the current two paths — build a generalized brain first or close the scenario loop first — both are logically valid, and it is impossible to judge in advance which is faster. By historical analogy, the auto industry had thousands of companies between 1900 and 1920, and only entered scale when Ford built the assembly line in 1913; robots have not yet reached their Model T moment, and whoever actually sells ten thousand robots first is already remarkable. But the better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented came countless categories — refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners — and robots interacting with the physical world will have N kinds of large scenarios, with home, companionship and industry each potentially producing their own native giant.

points.h: The incumbent who feels safe is the least safe
points.body: Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave no one is safe, and feeling safe is what makes you least safe. In business history no era's companies have ever transitioned smoothly into the next era; IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that overturns the industrial revolution, not a continuation-style innovation like mobile internet, so old giants' technology reserves and organizational culture are both negative assets. Google can live on as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is likewise not naturally safe. The new platform will most likely be created by a new company.

points.h: Human value lies in conjuring from nothing, not in writing songs or painting
points.body: Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the era of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI, and people are on one hand forced and on the other finally liberated to develop new potential. That potential is called creativity — not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and conjure something from nothing. AI has already taken away all existing knowledge, and human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. That is why he calls his own mission ‘to be a happy researcher’, and believes civilization will next reorganize around creativity, with even the education system forced to shift from ‘knowledge indoctrination’ to ‘open exploration’, because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

quotes.text: The most successful companies are certainly contrarian, but being contrarian does not guarantee success.
It may not survive to the end. It will probably do quite well going forward, but it is most likely not the big player, the big winner, of the native-application stage.
First-stage companies rarely survive into the second stage, and second-stage companies rarely survive into the third stage.
So companies will disappear, companies will die out. There is nothing to regret about that. There will be more fun things ahead — how many people are happy going to work at a company now? Not happy.

My technology is so good, I created so much value, why might my company be worth nothing? Because of the basic laws of economics: as long as there is homogeneous supply, you cannot capture high profits, and you are a company that isn't worth much.

Greatness is judged in hindsight, because you overcame negative feedback again and again, and when everyone disapproved of you, you finally proved through enormous success that you were the era's earliest prophet.
I have always felt that in the face of a giant wave no one is safe, and whoever feels safe is the least safe.
